title: Secrets: Vault and ExternalSecrets

story: The broker is ready to deploy, except for one thing: it needs the private key of our GitHub App, the key that lets it create a short-lived GitHub token for any repo the App is installed on. In p1-4 you learned that a key never goes into code. But the broker's unit in the infrastructure repo has a convenient env block, and a teammate suggests putting the key right there, "just for the first deploy".

Follow that key. It is now in git, forever, in a repo many people can read. It is in the plan that gets pasted into the pull request, where Byte, our review agent, and anyone with access read it. It is in the Terraform state file in S3, and in Helm's record of the release inside the cluster. One shortcut has made four copies of the most powerful key the platform holds, and none of them can be taken back.
hook.question: Where does a key live, and how does exactly one pod get exactly the key it needs, and nothing more?

p: The answer starts with one place for every secret: Vault, a secret store that runs on inf. Vault keeps secrets under paths, like folders, and for each path it keeps old versions, records who read what, and lets nobody read anything unless a policy allows it. A policy is a short rule in Vault that says which paths a login may read or write. Our secrets live in a part of Vault called kvv2, a key-value store with versions, and every tool on inf has its own folder: infrastructure/n8n for n8n, and infrastructure/ai-agents/broker, infrastructure/ai-agents/slack-app and so on for the agent platform.

A person puts a key in, once, over the VPN, and the way they type matters. A key written on the command line lands in the shell history and, while the command runs, in the list of processes that other programs can see. So the key is read from the keyboard without showing it, and handed to Vault through stdin, the input stream of a command. The =- at the end of the line means "take the value from stdin".

code.file: run once by a person on the VPN, in bash
code.text:
vault login -method=oidc

read -r -s -p "GitHub App key: " key; echo
printf '%s' "$key" | vault kv put -mount=kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/broker GITHUB_APP_KEY=-
unset key

vault kv get -mount=kvv2 -field=GITHUB_APP_KEY infrastructure/ai-agents/broker | wc -c

notes.text: Log in as yourself through the company login, so the audit log shows a person, not a shared password.
read -s does not show what you type, and the key lives only in a shell variable for a moment. This is bash syntax; in zsh, read -p means something else, so type bash first.
=- reads the value from stdin, so the key never appears in the command line, the history or the process list.
Check that something arrived by counting its characters, without printing the key on the screen.

read.h: A copy for one namespace: the ExternalSecret
p: The broker's pod needs the key as an environment variable, but a pod cannot simply ask Vault, because logging in to Vault needs a credential, and then that credential would need a home too. Instead, the cluster runs the External Secrets operator. An operator is a program that runs inside the cluster, watches objects of one kind, and acts on them. This one watches ExternalSecret objects. Each ExternalSecret says: copy this field from this Vault path into a normal Kubernetes Secret with this name, and check again every so often. The operator logs in to Vault through a store, an object that says where Vault is and how to log in, and writes the copy.

After that, the pod reads the Kubernetes Secret like any other, for example as an environment variable. The key never passed through git, a plan, Terraform state or Helm: the unit only names the path, and the path is not a secret.

code.text:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: broker
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  refreshInterval: 5m
  secretStoreRef:
    name: vault-store
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: broker
  data:
    - secretKey: GITHUB_APP_KEY
      remoteRef:
        key: infrastructure/ai-agents/broker
        property: GITHUB_APP_KEY

notes.text: Every 5 minutes the operator reads Vault again, so a new version of the key reaches the Secret without a deploy.
The store that logs in to Vault. Which store you name decides what this ExternalSecret is able to read; the next section is about that.
The Kubernetes Secret that the operator creates in the same namespace. The broker's Deployment reads this name.
Copy one field, and name it the way the program expects. Copy only what this pod needs.

deeper.h: Go deeper: base64 is not encryption, and env is read once
p: A Kubernetes Secret looks scrambled, GITHUB_APP_KEY: bGFiLW9ubHkta2V5LTE=, but that is base64, a way to write bytes as text, not encryption. Anyone allowed to read Secrets in the namespace can decode it with base64 -d. That is one more reason to keep the ai-agents namespace small and to copy only the fields a pod needs.

When the key changes in Vault, the operator updates the Secret within one refresh interval, but a running process read its environment variables when it started and will not see the change. The pod needs a restart, kubectl rollout restart, or the program must read the key from a mounted file instead. You will see both halves of this in the lab.

read.h: Narrow on purpose: who may read what
p: Now the part that is easy to miss. The ExternalSecret says what to copy, but the store's Vault login decides what may be copied. If the store's login is allowed to read all of kvv2, then any ExternalSecret that names that store, in any namespace, can copy any key in Vault into its own namespace. Somebody's small test service could ask for the Anthropic keys and get them.

On inf today, the shared store is called vault-store, and its login can read all of kvv2. That is a real gap, and it is honest to call it guidance, not a wall: what stops misuse today is that only DevOps can create ExternalSecrets on inf, through reviewed Terraform. The fix is a store of our own for the ai-agents namespace whose login has a policy that reads infrastructure/ai-agents/* and nothing else. Then an ExternalSecret for n8n's password, written in our namespace, fails with permission denied instead of quietly succeeding. You will make exactly that failure happen in the lab.

code.file: two Vault policies, narrow and wide

notes.text: kv-v2 paths have data/ after the mount name in policies. The * matches every secret in our folder.
Only read. The store never needs to write or delete.
This is what a store that reads everything amounts to: one login that can copy every key in the mount.

lab.title: A key travels from Vault into a pod
needs: The laptop cluster from p5-1, running (docker start academy)
About 500 MB of free memory in Docker
lab.goal: Put a key in Vault from stdin, let the External Secrets operator copy it into one pod, rotate it, and prove that a narrow policy refuses another tool's key.

guess.q: The store in ai-agents logs in with a token whose policy reads only infrastructure/ai-agents/*. Someone writes an ExternalSecret in ai-agents that asks for infrastructure/n8n. What happens?

options.text: It syncs, because the ExternalSecret is in a namespace that is allowed to have Secrets.
options.why: The namespace does not decide what Vault hands out. The store's login does, and its policy does not cover n8n's folder.

options.text: It fails with permission denied, and no Secret is created.
options.why: Vault checks the login's policy on every read. The ExternalSecret shows SecretSyncedError, and n8n's password never reaches our namespace.

options.text: Kubernetes refuses to create the ExternalSecret because the path is outside ai-agents.
options.why: Kubernetes does not know anything about Vault paths. The object is created fine; the read fails later, inside Vault.

follow.say: Point kubectl at your laptop cluster, then install the External Secrets operator with Helm. It takes about 40 seconds and adds the ExternalSecret and SecretStore kinds to the cluster.
follow.do: export KUBECONFIG=~/academy-k3s.yaml && helm repo add external-secrets https://charts.external-secrets.io && helm install external-secrets external-secrets/external-secrets --version 2.12.0 -n external-secrets --create-namespace --wait
follow.see:
"external-secrets" has been added to your repositories
NAME: external-secrets
NAMESPACE: external-secrets
STATUS: deployed
REVISION: 1
…
external-secrets has been deployed successfully in namespace external-secrets!

follow.say: Run a small Vault in the cluster. Dev mode keeps everything in memory and opens with a known root token, so it is only for labs. Wait about five seconds after this step, because Vault needs a moment to start listening.
follow.do: kubectl create namespace vault && kubectl -n vault run vault --image=hashicorp/vault:1.20.4 --port=8200 --expose --env=VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200 --env=VAULT_TOKEN=root -- vault server -dev -dev-root-token-id=root -dev-listen-address=0.0.0.0:8200 && kubectl -n vault wait pod/vault --for=condition=Ready --timeout=120s
follow.see:
namespace/vault created
service/vault created
pod/vault created
pod/vault condition met

follow.say: Create the kvv2 store like ours, then put the broker's key in from stdin, the way a person does it on the VPN. Also store a password for another tool, n8n, so you can try to steal it later.
follow.do: kubectl -n vault exec vault -- vault secrets enable -path=kvv2 kv-v2 && printf '%s' 'lab-only-key-1' | kubectl -n vault exec -i vault -- vault kv put -mount=kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/broker GITHUB_APP_KEY=- && printf '%s' 'n8n-lab-only' | kubectl -n vault exec -i vault -- vault kv put -mount=kvv2 infrastructure/n8n DB_PASSWORD=- > /dev/null
follow.see:
Success! Enabled the kv-v2 secrets engine at: kvv2/
============== Secret Path ==============
kvv2/data/infrastructure/ai-agents/broker
…
version            1

follow.say: Give our namespace a narrow login: a policy that reads only infrastructure/ai-agents/*, and a token with that policy, stored as a Secret for the store to use. The token travels through a pipe, so it is never printed.
follow.see:
Success! Uploaded policy: ai-agents-read
namespace/ai-agents created
secret/vault-token created

follow.say: Write the store and the broker's ExternalSecret into one file and apply it. The refresh interval is 10 seconds here instead of 5 minutes, so you do not have to wait in the rotation step.
follow.do:
cat > broker-secret.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: vault
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  provider:
    vault:
      server: http://vault.vault:8200
      path: kvv2
      version: v2
      auth:
        tokenSecretRef: { name: vault-token, key: token }
---
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: broker
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  refreshInterval: 10s
  secretStoreRef: { name: vault, kind: SecretStore }
  target:
    name: broker
  data:
    - secretKey: GITHUB_APP_KEY
      remoteRef:
        key: infrastructure/ai-agents/broker
        property: GITHUB_APP_KEY
EOF
kubectl apply -f broker-secret.yaml && sleep 8 && kubectl -n ai-agents get externalsecret
follow.see:
secretstore.external-secrets.io/vault created
externalsecret.external-secrets.io/broker created
NAME     STORETYPE     STORE   REFRESH INTERVAL   STATUS         READY
broker   SecretStore   vault   10s                SecretSynced   True

follow.say: Look at the Secret the operator made. The value looks scrambled, but it is only base64, so decode it.
follow.do: kubectl -n ai-agents get secret broker -o yaml | grep -A1 '^data:' && kubectl -n ai-agents get secret broker -o jsonpath='{.data.GITHUB_APP_KEY}' | base64 -d; echo

follow.say: Start a pod that reads the Secret as environment variables, the way the broker's pod does, and print the variable from inside it.
follow.do: kubectl -n ai-agents create deployment broker --image=busybox:1.37 -- sleep 86400 && kubectl -n ai-agents set env deployment/broker --from=secret/broker && kubectl -n ai-agents rollout status deployment/broker && kubectl -n ai-agents exec deploy/broker -- printenv GITHUB_APP_KEY
follow.see:
deployment.apps/broker created
deployment.apps/broker env updated
deployment "broker" successfully rolled out
lab-only-key-1

follow.say: Rotate the key in Vault, wait for one refresh, and compare the Secret with what the running pod sees.
follow.do: printf '%s' 'lab-only-key-2' | kubectl -n vault exec -i vault -- vault kv put -mount=kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/broker GITHUB_APP_KEY=- | grep version && sleep 12 && kubectl -n ai-agents get secret broker -o jsonpath='{.data.GITHUB_APP_KEY}' | base64 -d; echo; kubectl -n ai-agents exec deploy/broker -- printenv GITHUB_APP_KEY

follow.say: The Secret followed Vault, but the process still has the value it read at start. Restart the Deployment and look again.
follow.do: kubectl -n ai-agents rollout restart deployment/broker && kubectl -n ai-agents rollout status deployment/broker && kubectl -n ai-agents exec deploy/broker -- printenv GITHUB_APP_KEY
follow.see:
deployment.apps/broker restarted
deployment "broker" successfully rolled out
lab-only-key-2

follow.say: Now try to steal: ask for n8n's password from our namespace, through our store.
follow.do:
cat > grab-n8n.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: n8n-db
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  refreshInterval: 10s
  secretStoreRef: { name: vault, kind: SecretStore }
  target:
    name: n8n-db
  data:
    - secretKey: DB_PASSWORD
      remoteRef:
        key: infrastructure/n8n
        property: DB_PASSWORD
EOF
kubectl apply -f grab-n8n.yaml && sleep 8 && kubectl -n ai-agents get externalsecret n8n-db && kubectl -n ai-agents describe externalsecret n8n-db | grep -E 'Code: 403|permission denied'
follow.see:
externalsecret.external-secrets.io/n8n-db created
NAME     STORETYPE     STORE   REFRESH INTERVAL   STATUS              READY
n8n-db   SecretStore   vault   10s                SecretSyncedError   False
Code: 403. Errors:
  * permission denied

lab.build: The gateway needs Nova's Anthropic key, and only that one. In Vault, the path infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic holds one field per workload. Put a field nova in it from stdin, then add a second field routines with vault kv patch (put would replace the whole path). Write an ExternalSecret called gateway in ai-agents that copies only the nova field into a Secret called gateway, under the key ANTHROPIC_KEY_NOVA. Check that it syncs, and that the Secret holds exactly one key.
checks: kubectl -n ai-agents get externalsecret broker shows SecretSynced and READY True
The pod prints lab-only-key-1, and after the rotation and a restart it prints lab-only-key-2
Right after the rotation, the Secret already shows the new key while the running pod still prints the old one
The n8n-db ExternalSecret shows SecretSyncedError, and kubectl -n ai-agents get secret n8n-db says NotFound
kubectl -n ai-agents get secret gateway -o jsonpath='{.data}' shows only ANTHROPIC_KEY_NOVA, not the routines key

solution.file: the build: Vault commands and gateway.yaml
solution.text:
# 1. the key goes into Vault from stdin, never on the command line
printf '%s' 'lab-only-nova' | kubectl -n vault exec -i vault -- vault kv put -mount=kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic nova=-
printf '%s' 'lab-only-routines' | kubectl -n vault exec -i vault -- vault kv patch -mount=kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic routines=-

# 2. gateway.yaml: copy only the field the gateway needs
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: gateway
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  refreshInterval: 10s
  secretStoreRef: { name: vault, kind: SecretStore }
  target:
    name: gateway
  data:
    - secretKey: ANTHROPIC_KEY_NOVA
      remoteRef:
        key: infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic
        property: nova

lab.fix: A teammate got tired of permission errors and changed the store's token to the root token, "only for testing": printf root | kubectl -n ai-agents create secret generic vault-token --from-file=token=/dev/stdin --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -. Do the same, wait 15 seconds, and look at the n8n-db ExternalSecret: it now shows SecretSynced, and n8n's database password sits in our namespace. This is the vault-store gap from Understand, on your laptop. Put a narrow token back, delete the n8n-db ExternalSecret, and confirm that its Secret is gone too.
explain: Name the four places where the GitHub App key would have landed if it had gone into the unit's env block.
The ExternalSecret said what to copy, so what decided that n8n's password could not be copied?
After the rotation, why did the Secret show the new key while the running pod still printed the old one?
lab.done: A key went from stdin into Vault, from Vault into one Secret and one pod, followed a rotation, and a narrow policy refused another tool's key; when you finish p5, docker rm -f academy removes everything.

check.q: The Slack app's new bot token must reach its pod on inf. Which path is right?

options.text: Put it in the Slack app's unit as an env value, because the infrastructure repo is private
options.why: Private is not secret: the token would sit in git, in every pasted plan, in Terraform state and in Helm's release record.

options.text: A person writes it into Vault from stdin, and an ExternalSecret copies that one field into the Slack app's Secret
options.why: The value has one home, Vault, and one copy, in the namespace that needs it. The code only names the path.

options.text: Post it in the Jira ticket so DevOps can add it to the cluster by hand
options.why: Jira is read by people, search and agents. A key there is a leak with a timestamp, and a hand-made Secret has no owner in code.

check.q: On inf, an ExternalSecret in some other team's namespace asks vault-store for infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic. Why could it get our keys today?

options.text: Because the store's Vault login can read all of kvv2, and the store, not the ExternalSecret, decides what may be read
options.why: That is the gap. A store of our own with a policy for infrastructure/ai-agents/* only would turn this into permission denied.

options.text: Because Kubernetes Secrets are only base64
options.why: That is a different problem: reading a Secret that already exists. Here the question is who can create a copy from Vault in the first place.
Vault checks the policy of the login on every read. The problem is that this login's policy is too wide.

check.q: A key was rotated in Vault ten minutes ago. The broker's Secret already shows the new value, but the broker still fails with the old one. Why?

options.text: The operator has not refreshed the Secret yet
options.why: The Secret already shows the new value, so the operator did its part.

options.text: Vault keeps serving the old version for a day
options.why: Vault serves the latest version unless you ask for an older one.

options.text: The broker read its environment variables when it started, so it needs a restart to see the new value
options.why: Environment variables are fixed for the life of a process. A rollout restart, or reading the key from a mounted file, solves it.

p: Vault runs on inf at vault.rhinohealth.com with the kvv2 mount, and the agent platform's secrets live under infrastructure/ai-agents/: anthropic (one Anthropic key per workload, nova, routines and brain-bot, which only the gateway reads), gateway (the key that signs run tokens), temporal (the database password, generated straight into Vault by a secrets unit so no person ever sees it), broker (the GitHub App key and a database user), slack-app, orchestrator and jira-nova. Keys are written from stdin with metadata naming the owner, the reader and a 90-day rotation. Every service gets its copy through an ExternalSecret from its unit, and the VMs get no keys at all.

Two gaps are on the record. The shared ClusterSecretStore vault-store logs in with an AppRole that reads all of kvv2, so it goes on the threat model with an owner until a store of our own exists. And the Vault role that CI jobs use was open to any job in any of our repos with full admin rights; it is narrowed to the exact workflow files that need it before any agent pushes a branch, because a pushed branch runs CI.

tickets.why: Writes the Anthropic keys into Vault from stdin, one per workload, and records the vault-store gap.
The broker's, Slack app's and orchestrator's ExternalSecrets from their infrastructure/ai-agents/* paths.
Temporal's database password: generated into Vault by a secrets unit and copied by an ExternalSecret.
Narrows the CI Vault role to named workflow files before agents push branches.
The threat model, where the vault-store gap is written down with an owner.

words.plain: Our secret store on inf: secrets under paths, with versions, an audit log and policies.
A rule in Vault that says which paths a login may read or write.
A program inside the cluster that watches objects of one kind and acts on them.
An object asking the External Secrets operator to copy a field from Vault into a Kubernetes Secret.
A SecretStore or ClusterSecretStore: where Vault is and how to log in, which decides what can be copied.

review.q: Draw the key's path from a person's keyboard to the broker's process, and mark where it is a secret and where it is only a name.
review.a: Keyboard → stdin → Vault path (secret) → operator through the store's login → Kubernetes Secret (secret, base64) → environment variable of the pod. The unit and the ExternalSecret only hold the path, which is a name, not a secret.

review.q: What would you change on inf so that an ExternalSecret outside ai-agents can no longer copy the Anthropic keys?
review.a: A store of our own for the ai-agents namespace, with a login whose policy reads infrastructure/ai-agents/* only, and the agent services' ExternalSecrets pointing at it instead of vault-store.

review.q: Why does vault kv put use =- with printf instead of KEY=value?
review.a: A value on the command line lands in the shell history and in the process list. Through stdin it is never written anywhere but Vault.

remember: A key has one home, Vault; a pod gets a copy of only the field it needs through an ExternalSecret, and the store's policy decides how far that copying can reach.
